primary_meaning: In mainstream Christian interpretation, the seal or mark in the forehead symbolizes God's ownership of, identification with, and protection over His faithful people. It marks believers as belonging to God, secures them against divine judgment poured out on the wicked, and is commonly identified with the indwelling Holy Spirit and/or the name of God written on His servants, signifying allegiance, security of salvation, and consecration to God. Its placement on the forehead is widely read as signifying the mind—one's conscious loyalty, thought, and character being given to God (in deliberate contrast to the mark of the beast in Revelation 13).
primary_basis: Revelation 7:2-4 (the servants of God sealed in their foreheads before judgment)
Revelation 9:4 (those without the seal of God in their foreheads are harmed)
Revelation 14:1 (the Father's name written in the foreheads of the 144,000)
Revelation 22:4 (His name shall be in their foreheads)
Ezekiel 9:4-6 (a mark set on the foreheads of those who sigh over abominations, sparing them from slaughter)
Ephesians 1:13-14 and Ephesians 4:30 (believers sealed with the Holy Spirit)
2 Corinthians 1:21-22 (God has sealed us and given the Spirit as a guarantee)
2 Timothy 2:19 (the seal: 'The Lord knows those who are His')
Exodus 12:7,13 (blood on doorposts as protective mark, often cited as a type)

alternatives.meaning: The seal is specifically the Holy Spirit Himself: sealing is the Spirit's indwelling as a pledge/earnest of redemption, guaranteeing eternal security (emphasis in Reformed/evangelical soteriology, drawing Revelation together with the Pauline sealing texts).

The seal of God is the seventh-day Sabbath: observance of the Sabbath commandment (which contains God's name, title, and territory like an official seal) is the end-time sign of loyalty to God, in contrast to the mark of the beast (Sunday observance). Distinctive Seventh-day Adventist teaching.
basis: Exodus 20:8-11 (Sabbath command as containing the elements of a seal)
Ezekiel 20:12,20 (Sabbath as a sign between God and His people)

alternatives.meaning: The seal refers to baptism (and/or chrismation/confirmation): in patristic and Eastern Orthodox and Catholic sacramental tradition, 'the seal' (sphragis) is the sacramental sign impressed on the believer, marking them as Christ's own.
basis: Ephesians 1:13 as read by church fathers (e.g., Cyril of Jerusalem, Chrysostom)
Early liturgical usage of sphragis for baptism/chrismation

alternatives.meaning: A literal or visible eschatological mark: in some dispensationalist/futurist readings, the sealing of the 144,000 literal Jewish evangelists during a future tribulation is a real (possibly visible) protective mark applied at a specific future time.

Purely symbolic of settled character or the mind wholly devoted to God: the forehead represents the intellect/will, so the seal denotes a fixed, tested character or complete mental allegiance to God's truth, with no external mark of any kind implied.
basis: Revelation 14:1 and 22:4 (name in forehead as character/identity)
Deuteronomy 6:8 and 11:18 (God's words as frontlets between the eyes, i.e., in the mind)
Contrast with Revelation 13:16 mark of the beast as allegiance

notes: There is broad, recognizable consensus across Catholic, Orthodox, Protestant, and evangelical scholarship on the core meaning: the seal marks God's people as His own, protecting them from eschatological judgment, with the forehead signifying the mind/allegiance. The alternatives differ mainly on the referent or mechanism of the seal (Holy Spirit, baptism, Sabbath, literal future mark) rather than on the basic ownership-and-protection symbolism, which nearly all traditions share. The Ezekiel 9 background and the deliberate antithesis with the mark of the beast (Revelation 13:16-17) are near-universally noted in commentaries (e.g., Beale, Mounce, Osborne, Aune, Caird). The Sabbath-as-seal reading is confessionally distinctive to Seventh-day Adventism and not accepted in wider scholarship; the sacramental (baptismal) reading is historically significant in patristic literature but is a minority framing in modern exegesis of Revelation itself.
